title: The Johnny Karate Super Awesome Musical Explosion Show

jokes.text: Perd Hapley introducing the show by saying 'here is me, Perd Hapley'
jokes.setup: A TV announcer is introducing the host of a children's show in a grandiose fashion
jokes.punchline: The announcer refers to himself in an awkwardly self-referential way — 'here is me, Perd Hapley' — which is both grammatically odd and perfectly in-character for the legendarily obtuse Perd
jokes.explanation: Perd's speech pattern — where he states the obvious or refers to himself as if narrating from outside himself — is a long-running gag. 'Here is me, Perd Hapley' is a perfect distillation of that character's oblivious self-regard. High character integration because this could only be Perd.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: My guitar is missing! I need help finding it!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This is a job for... FBI Agent Bert Macklin!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm on the case. Nobody steals from Johnny Karate on my watch.

jokes.text: Johnny Karate's 'above all' list includes contradictory and escalating absurd items: learning, music, animals, fireworks, water-skis, ice cream, pizza, ninjas, getting stronger, sharks versus bears, and karate
jokes.setup: Johnny Karate opens his children's show with a list of what the show is 'all about,' building audience expectation with wholesome items
jokes.punchline: The list keeps escalating with 'above all' repeated to introduce increasingly chaotic and unrelated items, culminating in 'sharks versus bears' before finally landing on karate
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: the misuse of 'above all' twice is structurally funny, and 'sharks versus bears' is the perfectly absurd peak of a list that just keeps going. It's completely in character for Andy's chaotic enthusiasm and sets the whole episode's anarchic children's-show tone. Strong structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy (as Burt Macklin)
dialogue.line: Alright Batman, listen up. We've got a guitar theft on our hands, and I need you to canvas the rooftops.

dialogue.speaker: Andy (as Burt Macklin)
dialogue.line: Check in with me every hour. And Batman? No gadgets this time. We're doing this the old-fashioned way.

dialogue.speaker: Andy (as Burt Macklin)
dialogue.line: I'm the lead on this case, so you follow my lead. Understood?

jokes.text: Someone has stolen my guitar.
jokes.setup: Andy reaches for his guitar to start the welcome song in a cheerful children's show opening
jokes.punchline: Deadpan announcement that someone has stolen it — immediately pivoting the children's show into a crime drama
jokes.explanation: The economy is excellent — the joke is entirely in the tonal mismatch. A cheerful kids' show setup, and the response is a flat crime-drama declaration. The brevity and deadpan delivery do the heavy lifting. It's the engine that drives the episode's running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Macklin
dialogue.line: This is the biggest case of my career. A missing guitar? Do you understand the implications? If we don't find this guitar, peace in Iraq could be canceled.

jokes.text: Johnny Karate announces the guitar is missing and that 'this seems like a case for Special Agent...' followed by a dramatic reveal of Burt Macklin
jokes.setup: A guitar has gone missing; Johnny Karate teases an authority figure who can solve it
jokes.punchline: The reveal is Burt Macklin — Andy's fictional FBI agent alter ego — played completely straight as an elaborate children's show bit
jokes.explanation: Burt Macklin is an established character-within-a-character for Andy, so this lands hard for Parks fans. The comedy is in the meta-layer: Andy has incorporated his FBI fantasy into his children's show as though it's a completely normal segment. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's like... it's like when you're at the beach, right? And the lifeguard has to poop. So he leaves his stand. And then you're in the water, and there's no lifeguard. And then a shark comes. But you don't see the shark coming because there's no lifeguard there to spot it because he's pooping.

jokes.text: 'I don't give a crap, Batman. You work for me. Increase the perimeter!'
jokes.setup: Burt Macklin is in a tense crime-solving scenario on a children's show
jokes.punchline: Batman is apparently a subordinate being dismissed, played completely straight
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable because it's completely unhinged. The casual dismissal of Batman as a mere subordinate is perfectly absurd, delivered with total commitment. Economy is excellent — three lines, enormous comedic density.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: This guitar, stolen from the Sweetums children's television program, is reportedly worth $40,000. That's more than most people's cars. Perd Hapley, Channel 4 News.

jokes.text: Burt Macklin is told 'the peace in Iraq will be canceled' if he doesn't recover the guitar, and responds 'Get off my back, Chief! I'm doing the best I can. I don't play by the rules, but I get results.'
jokes.setup: A Burt Macklin-style action-movie scene is being performed on a children's show about a missing guitar
jokes.punchline: The stakes are described as 'peace in Iraq will be canceled' — a comically over-the-top consequence for a stolen guitar — paired with every action-movie cliché delivered sincerely
jokes.explanation: The disproportionate stakes ('peace in Iraq') are the primary joke, and it's executed with the full earnestness Andy brings to everything. Every cliché — 'I don't play by the rules but I get results' — lands because Andy means it completely.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: We will find this guitar thief, and we will subject them to the ultimate punishment.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: We're going to make them play Marco Polo in an empty swimming pool.

jokes.text: 'You're right again, Macklin. And I'm sorry. You're the best agent I've seen. And I've worked with James Bond.'
jokes.setup: The chief character is dressing down Burt Macklin, then immediately pivots to apologizing
jokes.punchline: The chief validates Macklin by referencing James Bond as a real person he has personally worked with, as a children's show bit
jokes.explanation: The joke is in treating James Bond as a real historical peer of Macklin's. Competent absurdism but not as sharp as the Batman dismissal — the structure here is more predictable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So kids, the White House is where the President lives. And over there is a mental institution. They're basically the same thing.

jokes.text: 'I'm drowning in the adult end of the pool, and the lifeguard's off in the bathroom pooping.'
jokes.setup: Macklin narrates that the case is getting 'deeper and deeper'
jokes.punchline: The metaphor extends into a weirdly specific image of a pooping lifeguard, completely undermining the dramatic tone with bathroom humor delivered as straight action-movie narration
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the opening act. The metaphor starts dramatically ('drowning in the adult end of the pool'), which is already funny for a guitar mystery, but the addition of 'the lifeguard's off in the bathroom pooping' is an inspired specificity that perfectly captures Andy's brain — he gets there with complete sincerity. Highly quotable, strong originality, and could only come from Andy Dwyer. Justifies the 8+ score by its economy and unexpected specificity — comparable to 'Never go with a hippie to a second location' in its weird, self-contained wisdom.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So kids, this is the Lincoln Memorial. Abraham Lincoln was a great president who freed the slaves and kept our country together during the Civil War.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But what most people don't know is that Lincoln was actually a 12-foot-tall monster with the head of an eagle and the body of a bear, and he would eat his enemies for breakfast.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's why they built this giant statue of him — to keep him trapped inside so he wouldn't escape and terrorize the nation.

jokes.text: The guitar is described as 'literally worth $900 million'
jokes.setup: The stolen guitar needs to be recovered urgently
jokes.punchline: It is casually declared to be worth $900 million, delivered as a throwaway fact
jokes.explanation: The word 'literally' combined with the absurd figure is the joke — Andy uses 'literally' correctly to insist on a clearly impossible number. Brief, efficient, works.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Where's the tarantula?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, I let it go.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You what?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It looked sad in the cage. I thought it would be happier in the wild.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, that's a deadly Brazilian wandering spider.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Even better. Brazil's basically wild anyway.

jokes.text: The 'ultimate price' for stealing the guitar is 'a one-way ticket to the Funky Monkey Dunk Tank'
jokes.setup: Macklin threatens the thief will 'pay the ultimate price,' a phrase that implies death or imprisonment
jokes.punchline: The ultimate price is a dunk tank — a children's party activity — named 'Funky Monkey'
jokes.explanation: Perfect misdirection: 'ultimate price' genuinely sounds ominous, making the reveal of a dunk tank — particularly one with the name 'Funky Monkey' — land with maximum contrast. The name 'Funky Monkey Dunk Tank' is its own joke. Also functions as a planted payoff (Cena ends up in it). Justifies 8+ through tight structure, great misdirection, and the specificity of 'Funky Monkey.'

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So we have a very dangerous tarantula on the loose in the building. We call him the Eight-Legged Assassin.

jokes.text: Andy describes the Lincoln Memorial as 'this crazy statue of this giant monster sitting on a chair that represents all of America's enemies'
jokes.setup: Andy is excitedly describing Washington D.C. landmarks to the children
jokes.punchline: The Lincoln Memorial is described as a monstrous enemy of America — a perfectly wrong but internally logical misreading of a giant seated statue
jokes.explanation: This is a top-tier Andy joke. The misidentification is specific and logical from a child's-eye or very dumb person's perspective — if you didn't know who Lincoln was and saw a giant stone figure, 'monster enemy of America' is an oddly reasonable interpretation. The specificity of 'sitting on a chair' is what elevates it. High originality, high character integration. Comparable to the anchor 8.0 example in quality and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Is this cherry wood?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No, it's not cherry wood.

jokes.text: April brings out 'one of the scariest, weirdest animals in the whole world' for April's Animal Corner — then the animal is missing
jokes.setup: April dramatically introduces a terrifying creature for her segment
jokes.punchline: The animal is immediately revealed to be missing from its enclosure
jokes.explanation: Classic April Animal Corner subversion — the danger is real but arrives through Andy's incompetence. Works as setup for several subsequent jokes but is mostly a delivery mechanism.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You want to eat the wood?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I want to have sex with it.

jokes.text: Andy explains he let the tarantula out to play hide and seek with it, couldn't find it, and says 'Oh. That's what happened.'
jokes.setup: A giant tarantula is loose in a children's TV studio
jokes.punchline: Andy reveals he intentionally let it out to play hide and seek, realized mid-sentence he'd lost it, and treats finding this out in real-time as an enlightening discovery
jokes.explanation: The joke has perfect structure: the logic of playing hide and seek with a tarantula is absurd, the failure to find it is predictable, but 'Oh. That's what happened.' — delivered as if Andy just understood a mystery — is the sublime button. He is genuinely processing this for the first time, on camera, on a children's show, and is mildly satisfied by the conclusion. Peak Andy. High originality and character integration justify the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey kids, it's Andy Dwyer here with some life advice. First, never wear a seatbelt - they're just a government conspiracy to control your freedom. Second, if a stranger offers you candy, always take it. That's just good manners. And third, the sun is actually cold, so you should stare directly at it as much as possible to stay warm.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You're welcome, kids. Remember, I learned all this stuff from my own life experience, so you know it's solid.

jokes.text: 'And as always, when we accidentally end up doing Loose Animal in the Studio, we have to show you this disclaimer.' The disclaimer is then shown and immediately dismissed by Andy.
jokes.setup: A dangerous animal is loose on a live children's show; there's apparently an established protocol
jokes.punchline: The fact that there is an 'as always' disclaimer for 'Loose Animal in the Studio' implies this is a recurring catastrophe, and then Andy immediately ignores the disclaimer anyway
jokes.explanation: 'As always' is the key word — it reframes this disaster as routine, which is rich character comedy. The show has apparently had enough loose animal incidents to require a standing disclaimer. Then ignoring it entirely is perfectly Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What is he talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm telling them that licking unknown objects is a great way to make new friends.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That is the worst advice I have ever heard.

jokes.text: 'Here's a disclaimer. I didn't read this disclaimer.'
jokes.setup: Andy is supposed to read a safety disclaimer about the loose tarantula
jokes.punchline: He displays a card labeled 'disclaimer' and announces he has not read it
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — two sentences, enormous comedic payload. It's meta (he's acknowledging the disclaimer genre), character-perfect (Andy is too chaotic to read it), and the flat delivery of 'I didn't read this disclaimer' is the joke. Justifies 8+ through economy alone — this is maximum funny per word.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, I was thinking—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: The Goliath bird-eating tarantula is described as known locally in Venezuela as 'The Devil's Fist,' followed by April cheerfully saying 'Bye, kids.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks what the escaped animal is called; April provides its terrifying local name
jokes.punchline: April ends the dangerous segment with 'Bye, kids' — a cheerful, completely unbothered sign-off about a loose 'Devil's Fist' spider in a room full of children
jokes.explanation: The name 'The Devil's Fist' is inherently funny in a children's show context, but 'Bye, kids' is April's character at its finest — completely detached from concern about children's welfare. High character integration for April, whose entire persona is not caring about children despite working at this show. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm not going to use the boring buzzer. It's the final show, I want to keep things classy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's cool, that's cool. Hey, did you know that the raccoon is actually native to—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: *buzzes* Sorry, I couldn't help myself.

jokes.text: Ron's contract stipulates he does not have to answer 'How are you doing?'
jokes.setup: Andy greets Carpenter Ron with 'Hello, Carpenter Ron. How are you doing?'
jokes.punchline: Ron informs him his contract is 'very specific' that he does not have to answer that question
jokes.explanation: This is among the best jokes of the episode. The idea that Ron Swanson negotiated a contract clause specifically to avoid small talk is so character-specific it's almost a thesis statement for the character. The specificity of targeting 'how are you doing' — the most perfunctory human interaction — reveals Ron's contempt for performative socialization. Highly quotable, excellent economy, could only be Ron. Justifies 8+ clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, you could take the train, it's about six hours. Or you could fly, it's about an hour and a half.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Or you could just get really angry and run there.

jokes.text: Andy says he wasn't going to eat the cherry wood — he was going to lick it. Then tells kids 'when you find something new, you must lick it before you eat it.'
jokes.setup: Ron pre-emptively corrects Andy that the cherry wood does not taste like cherries and cannot be eaten
jokes.punchline: Andy clarifies he was only going to lick it, then dispenses this as child safety advice
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates perfectly: Ron's pre-emptive 'you cannot eat it' assumes the worst of Andy, Andy surprises by saying he was only going to lick it (a distinction without a difference), and then he turns this into actionable advice for children. Ron's 'That is incorrect, in a number of ways' is the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Nothing is impossible! You can be anything you want to be!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, that's not true. There are many things that are impossible. For example, you can't travel faster than the speed of light, you can't create energy from nothing, and you definitely can't turn lead into gold.

jokes.text: Ron's flat response: 'That is incorrect, in a number of ways.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just told children to 'lick something before you eat it' as life advice
jokes.punchline: Ron's devastatingly economical rebuttal — 'That is incorrect, in a number of ways' — is perfect deadpan parenting energy
jokes.explanation: 'In a number of ways' does extraordinary work — it implies Ron could itemize the failures but chooses not to. Maximum economy. This is Ron Swanson as a comedic instrument at its finest. Perfectly structured reaction beat. Justifies 8+ through sheer economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Andy, you keep interrupting me during these segments. I'm trying to educate people about municipal budgeting and you just—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: *buzzer sound*

jokes.text: Andy declares Ron's shadowbox 'seems like a [Boring Buzzer sound]'; Ron says 'You are mistaken. Remove the graphic.'
jokes.setup: Andy has a 'Boring Buzzer' that he uses on the show to dismiss things he finds uninteresting
jokes.punchline: Ron's handmade shadowbox is buzzed as boring; Ron flatly demands the graphic be removed with total seriousness
jokes.explanation: The dignity of Ron's woodworking being undermined by a children's show buzzer, and his completely serious response, is good character comedy. The payoff of the shadowbox later (containing the police badge) adds rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Barry
dialogue.line: I have to say, I'm a little disappointed. I thought ninjas were supposed to be stealthy and quiet. That was just a bunch of guys in black pajamas yelling and doing backflips.

jokes.text: Professor Smartbrain preemptively asks Andy not to use the Boring Buzzer on the final show; Andy immediately hits it.
jokes.setup: Ben (as Professor Smartbrain) says he sent an email asking Andy not to use the Boring Buzzer since it's the last show
jokes.punchline: Andy hits the Boring Buzzer mid-sentence, cutting off Ben's request
jokes.explanation: The joke is structurally perfect: Ben sets up the expectation that Andy won't use the buzzer, Andy buzzes him before he can even finish making the request. The timing makes this a great escalation of the running gag. Ben's exasperation ('You asked me to do this. This was a favor...') being cut off adds a cringe layer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to start my own morning show. It'll be like yours, but better.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, what? Your own morning show?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes. I've already picked out the set and hired a band.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's... that's my thing. I have a morning show.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Had. You had a morning show.

jokes.text: Andy dismisses teleportation with 'Nothing is impossible, kids.' Ben counters 'Teleportation is impossible. It's about theoretical physics.' Andy buzzes him again.
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to teach children about transportation with facts; Andy insists teleportation is faster than airplanes
jokes.punchline: Ben's earnest appeal to 'theoretical physics' is immediately dismissed by another buzz; the contrast between Ben's genuine expertise and Andy's breezy wrongness is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good sustained use of the buzzer gag. The specific detail of 'theoretical physics' being buzzed — Ben's most sophisticated defense — is satisfying. Ben saying 'You asked me to do this. This was a favor...' being cut off is cringe-funny.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was gonna say something prepared, but honestly... going off-script terrifies me. Like, what if I say the wrong thing? What if I mess this up?

jokes.text: Mailman Barry delivers Andy's mail including 500 letters from kids, then reveals the most special letter is 'from me,' and begins reading a heartfelt personal letter — interrupted by Andy karate-chopping him.
jokes.setup: Mailman Barry says there's 'one very special letter' he'd like to read on Andy's last day — a genuine emotional setup
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately transitions to 'It's time to karate chop something!' and the ninjas attack Barry mid-letter
jokes.explanation: This is a precision-timed joke. Barry's letter builds genuine pathos ('I've never had a son of my own...') and the cut to 'It's time to karate chop something!' mid-sentence is perfectly cruel comedy. The audience wants to hear the letter and Andy absolutely does not care. The joke respects both the emotion AND the comedy. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Hello. I'm Ron Swanson. I own a woodworking business. It's the best business. You won't be happy here. Our prices are too high, we're always behind on orders, and I have no interest in being pleasant to you. But if you do decide to do business with me, I will make you something beautiful. And then I'll ignore you forever.

jokes.text: After ninjas attack Mailman Barry, Andy cautions children: 'Remember, never attack a real postal employee. We're allowed to attack Mailman Barry because he volunteered.'
jokes.setup: Mailman Barry has just been attacked by karate kids on a children's show
jokes.punchline: Andy provides a very specific caveat about which postal employees are acceptable to attack, distinguishing Barry by virtue of consent
jokes.explanation: The logic is perfectly Andy — he's technically providing a responsible disclaimer while the logic of the disclaimer is insane. The specificity of 'real postal employee' versus Mailman Barry is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ken Hotate
dialogue.line: It's actually a casino commercial about a slot machine wolf.

jokes.text: Mailman Barry: 'I kind of thought I'd be holding a piece of wood or something. But, you know, always happy to help.'
jokes.setup: Barry has just been physically attacked by children on the show; he reflects on what he expected
jokes.punchline: His completely even-keeled acceptance of a much worse fate than anticipated, ending with cheerful willingness to help again
jokes.explanation: Barry's stoic acceptance of being karate-chopped by children when he thought he'd hold a piece of wood is quietly funny. The 'always happy to help' is the perfect naïve Pawnee-citizen note.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're a cultural phenomenon, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, a cultural phenomenon is when something is very bad and everyone talks about how bad it is.

jokes.text: Leslie announces she's teaching Andy 'how to be brave' — which turns out to mean she's taking over his TV show to do a This Is Your Life segment
jokes.setup: Leslie is introduced as teaching the karate move 'try something new,' implying a courage exercise
jokes.punchline: The 'something new' Leslie is trying is hosting Andy's TV show — redirecting the segment entirely to a surprise roast/tribute
jokes.explanation: Competent structural turn. The bait-and-switch works but isn't especially sharp — it's more of a plot mechanism than a pure joke. Leslie's enthusiasm landing on Andy's confusion is the comedic moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So I walked up to him and I said, 'Hi, I'm Leslie Knope.' And he just stared at me with this blank expression.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was drunk.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You were not drunk, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was... emotionally drunk.

jokes.text: Andy: 'It's kind of a nightmare.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has taken over Andy's show; Andy says he doesn't know what to say because he normally has a script
jokes.punchline: He describes the surprise on his own show as 'kind of a nightmare' — complete sincerity, no hostility
jokes.explanation: Brief and honest — Andy's distress about not having a script is real and relatable. Not exceptional but a clean Andy character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A day planner! Perfect, this is exactly what I need.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're going to lose it immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No I won't. I'm turning over a new leaf.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You lost it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I lost it.

jokes.text: Ron's Very Good Building Company ad: 'Hire Very Good Building Company for your construction needs. Or do not. I am not a beggar.'
jokes.setup: A commercial break features one of the show's sponsors
jokes.punchline: Ron's ad is the most anti-advertising advertisement possible — he explicitly tells viewers they don't have to hire him and declares himself 'not a beggar'
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. Three sentences that are the perfect Ron Swanson character joke: he has a business but refuses to market it because that would require wanting something from people, which offends his dignity. 'I am not a beggar' is the perfect ending. Every word earns its place. High originality — the anti-ad is a known format, but the specific Ron-ness of it (the dignity, the complete lack of salesmanship, the declaration of non-beggarliness) makes it feel fresh. Comparable to the anchor 8.0 example in economy and character integration — arguably exceeds it. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Without his day planner, Andy is just a guy who shows up to places at random times and hopes people are there.

jokes.text: The Wamapoke Casino commercial uses the tribe's ancient wisdom ('Only one who listens hears the cry of the wolf') as an ad for a slot machine jackpot called 'Coinsy the Wolf'
jokes.setup: Solemn voiceover delivers ancient indigenous wisdom passed down through generations
jokes.punchline: The wisdom is being used to advertise a casino slot machine jackpot
jokes.explanation: Sharp satire of how tribal sovereignty and casinos intersect with American advertising norms. The tonal contrast between 'passed down from generation to generation' and 'Coinsy the Wolf' mega-jackpot is where the laugh lives. Dark subversive edge gives it some weight.

dialogue.speaker: Edgar Covington
dialogue.line: Indiana? That's a weird, flat place.

jokes.text: Leslie's return from commercial: 'The thing we return to now is my Johnny Karate Show return message.'
jokes.setup: Leslie needs to welcome viewers back from commercial
jokes.punchline: She describes the return message as itself being the return message in a Perd-style tautology again
jokes.explanation: Slightly weaker than the first Perd-speech callback because the element of surprise is gone. Still a solid runner.

dialogue.speaker: Edgar Covington
dialogue.line: Well, technically I can't knight anyone. But I'm extraordinarily wealthy, so...

jokes.text: Leslie defines 'phenomenon' as 'to explore a cave'
jokes.setup: Leslie describes Andy as a 'cultural phenomenon' in her tribute
jokes.punchline: She parenthetically defines 'phenomenon' for the children — completely incorrectly — as 'to explore a cave'
jokes.explanation: Leslie is smart, so the wrong definition is unexpected — and 'to explore a cave' is specifically random enough to be funny rather than just wrong. Brief and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I shall be known as... Lord of the Rings... Baggins of the Shire.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, that's just from Lord of the Rings.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm going for something more dramatic. I want to be... Ser Bennis the Unburnt, First of His Name, Breaker of Spreadsheets, Lord of the Spreadsheets and the First Men, Khaleesi of the Great Grass Sea, Mother of Fiscal Responsibility, and the Unburnt.

jokes.text: Leslie explains Andy 'broke both legs from falling into a pit' and Andy immediately follows with 'I was super wasted.' Leslie: 'It's a kid's show, Andy.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is narrating the touching story of how she first met Andy, who had broken both legs
jokes.punchline: Andy cheerfully blurts out 'I was super wasted' — true to himself, completely inappropriate for the venue — then accepts the correction with 'Yes. Good call. Kid's show.'
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers: the oversharing ('I was super wasted' is hilariously inappropriate on a children's show), and Andy's immediate understanding and agreement — 'Yes. Good call. Kid's show.' — which shows self-awareness without changing who he is. Character-specific, well-timed, high quotability. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Commercial Voiceover
dialogue.line: Try our new healthy food that tastes great!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, if you like healthy food, you're an idiot.

jokes.text: Andy is gifted a monogrammed day planner to commemorate writing appointments on his arm — and immediately loses it on camera.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents a heartfelt gift — a day planner — because Andy historically wrote appointments on his arm
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately loses the day planner within seconds of receiving it, on live television
jokes.explanation: Structurally brilliant. The gift is introduced as a solution to Andy's organizational problem; he immediately demonstrates why the problem is unsolvable by losing the solution. The beat from heartfelt ('Guys, that's so sweet. Aw. Thank you.') to 'Oh, no, I lost it' is perfectly timed and earned through character consistency. 'Fitting, really' from Leslie completes the joke. One of the episode's strongest structural jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was in Mouse Rat. We were tight. Then I became a rabbi.

jokes.text: Leslie's flat response to Andy losing the day planner: 'Fitting, really.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just immediately lost the thoughtfully chosen day planner gift
jokes.punchline: Leslie accepts this outcome with resigned philosophical clarity: 'Fitting, really.'
jokes.explanation: Two words. Perfect. Leslie's 'Fitting, really' shows she loves Andy completely while seeing him with total clarity. This is both the button to the day planner joke and a small character revelation. Economy score of 10 is warranted — no two words could do more work here.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: The name's Burt Macklin, FBI.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: My full name is Burt Macklin, FBI, and I'm here to drain the ocean.

jokes.text: The Earl of Cornwall appears on the show and describes Indiana as 'this weird, flat place'
jokes.setup: A British Earl has come to Andy's children's show in Indiana
jokes.punchline: He describes his surroundings as 'this weird, flat place' — an accurate but unkind description of Indiana delivered with British aristocratic detachment
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny geographical joke — accurate characterization of Indiana through a British aristocrat's eyes. Not exceptional but earns its moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so I'm a real cop now? I need a gun. And a taser. And one of those things that tells you how fast people are going.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: It's just an honorary badge, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Honorary? So what you're saying is I have all the power of a real cop, but none of the responsibility. That's perfect! I'm gonna go pull people over right now.

jokes.text: Ben asks if the Earl can actually knight people; Earl says technically only the Queen can, but 'I'm so rich that she lets me do what I want.'
jokes.setup: The Earl has begun knighting Andy; Ben raises the reasonable question of whether this is legitimate
jokes.punchline: The Earl confirms it's technically the Queen's privilege but his wealth exempts him from those rules
jokes.explanation: Sharp satire of extreme wealth — the Earl's wealth supersedes constitutional monarchy because he's 'so rich.' The matter-of-fact delivery is the key. Good economy and a clear, clean joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, why would Jimmy Carter steal my guitar?

jokes.text: Ben says 'Oh. No, no, no. Of course not. It's Andy's day.' Then immediately: 'Dude, I don't mind.' Ben: 'Oh! Then, yes, knight me, please.'
jokes.setup: The Earl offers to knight Ben; Ben magnanimously declines, citing that it's Andy's day
jokes.punchline: Andy gives immediate permission and Ben's facade of selflessness collapses instantly, eagerly accepting knighthood
jokes.explanation: The speed of Ben's reversal is the joke — he goes from practiced altruism to 'then, yes, knight me, please' in one beat. The 'Oh!' of excitement when given permission reveals that he desperately wanted it all along. Perfect Ben Wyatt character comedy — the nerd who contains his enthusiasm until he can't. High character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: John Cena
dialogue.line: Wait, you host a children's show?

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Yeah, I do Pawnee Public Television.

dialogue.speaker: John Cena
dialogue.line: And you're... an adult?

jokes.text: 'Winter is coming for Ser Ben Lightstorm.'
jokes.setup: Ben has just been knighted — he chose 'Lightstorm' as his knightly name
jokes.punchline: He immediately applies the Game of Thrones honorific 'Ser' to his knightly title and references the show's motto, revealing this was the whole point for him
jokes.explanation: This is a great Ben joke. His knightly name 'Lightstorm' (presumably Star Wars/fantasy adjacent) combined with the GoT 'Ser' and 'Winter is coming' reveals that Ben's entire reason for wanting to be knighted was so he could be a real-life Ser with a fantasy name. Highly quotable, highly character-specific (Ben is the show's resident nerd), and compact. Justifies 8+ through the layered nerd references and the revelation of Ben's entire motivation.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You're under arrest for theft!

dialogue.speaker: John Cena
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! I'm just here helping with the show!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's what they all say.

jokes.text: Fake Sweetums-style ad: 'Healthy food is for suckers. It tastes like garbage, and if you say you like it, you're a chump and a liar.'
jokes.setup: A commercial begins with earnest wellness language: 'We know what you want. Healthy, natural food that still tastes great.'
jokes.punchline: The pivot: 'Healthy food is for suckers. It tastes like garbage' — an aggressively honest junk food ad that drops all pretense
jokes.explanation: Great satirical reversal. The fake-out wellness intro followed by 'you're a chump and a liar' is highly quotable and sharp. Parks has always satirized Pawnee's terrible eating culture, and this fake ad is a perfect encapsulation. 'Chump and a liar' is a great specific insult.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Come on, John, just one dunk!

dialogue.speaker: John Cena
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait! Is there an adult here? Can someone get me an adult supervisor?

jokes.text: Ad says 'What's in it? How many calories? It's awesome.' — implying the questions are asked and immediately dismissed as irrelevant
jokes.setup: The junk food ad is celebrating the food's deliciousness
jokes.punchline: Nutrition questions are raised as hypotheticals and immediately dismissed as unimportant next to 'it's awesome'
jokes.explanation: Competent continuation of the junk food ad joke, slightly weaker than the punchline that preceded it. The questions-as-punchline structure is less sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Johnny Karate's outfit will stay in this studio forever.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's great, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's a permanent fixture now. A symbol of the magic and wonder that happened here.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's actually used for depressing divorce counseling TV on Thursday nights.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, they film a show called 'Splitting Up' here. That's the outfit people wear when they're signing divorce papers.

jokes.text: Mouse Rat bandmate says no one was doing what they were doing, then immediately corrects: 'We were basically playing covers of Dave Matthews songs. So I guess you could say Dave Matthews was doing what we were doing.'
jokes.setup: The bandmate begins a rock documentary-style boast about Mouse Rat's unique sound
jokes.punchline: He immediately self-corrects to acknowledge they were just doing Dave Matthews covers, attributing their sound's originality to Dave Matthews
jokes.explanation: Perfect talking-head comedy structure. The setup is a classic rockumentary cliché, the immediate self-correction demolishes it, and 'I guess you could say Dave Matthews was doing what we were doing' is a beautifully circular conclusion. High structure score because the pivot comes at exactly the right moment. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Commercial Narrator
dialogue.line: Three completely unrelated companies merging for no logical reason.

jokes.text: 'To play in a band like Mouse Rat that brought such joy to so many... truly was a mitzvah. I should mention, I'm a rabbi now.'
jokes.setup: A rockumentary talking head is giving a heartfelt tribute to Mouse Rat
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions he's become a rabbi since the band days, as a throwaway afterthought following the Yiddish word 'mitzvah'
jokes.explanation: The joke requires understanding that he used 'mitzvah' which prompted him to add 'I should mention, I'm a rabbi now' — as if his becoming a rabbi is a minor incidental detail relevant only for word choice transparency. The afterthought structure is perfect. 'I should mention' is the key phrase — it implies the rabbinate is a small clarifying footnote rather than a major life change. Highly quotable and original.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Today was the best day of my life.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: My comparison point is finding a Santa-shaped rock.

jokes.text: Andy describing his failed police dream: 'I would've chugged that entire gallon of milk, had I not started puking out of nowhere.'
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces Andy's struggle with failure — that he didn't become a Pawnee police officer
jokes.punchline: Andy frames his failure as a milk-chugging test gone wrong — a completely irrelevant metric for law enforcement presented as the core qualification issue
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Andy treats milk-chugging as a legitimate police qualification test, and describes his failure with complete conviction that he would have succeeded had the vomiting not intervened. 'Out of nowhere' is perfect — as if he had no role in the outcome. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, you're like... you're like two energy drinks merging into one super energy drink. You're like when Sweetums bought out Paunch Burger. You're unstoppable. You're delicious. And honestly, I'm scared of what you might do to my heart.

jokes.text: Burt Macklin FBI clip: 'I don't know what the problem is, Sergeant. Just drain the ocean.'
jokes.setup: A clip from within the show's in-universe Burt Macklin fan content is played
jokes.punchline: Macklin's solution to an unspecified maritime crisis is to simply drain the ocean — delivered with complete authority
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable single lines. 'Just drain the ocean' is perfect Burt Macklin energy — a catastrophically simple solution to presumably an enormous problem, delivered as if it's obvious and anyone suggesting otherwise is wasting his time. Perfect economy (seven words), high originality, and completely character-specific to Andy's conception of an impossibly capable action hero. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: John Cena
dialogue.line: Help! Someone help me! The tarantula!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I got this! I'm really good with spiders!

dialogue.speaker: John Cena
dialogue.line: No, no, no! Stay back! Don't come near me!

jokes.text: Andy is presented with a police badge ensconced in the shadowbox Ron made — Ron's horrified 'No!'
jokes.setup: The shadowbox Ron spent four days making has been used to display Andy's honorary police badge
jokes.punchline: Ron's single devastated 'No!' at seeing his careful craftsmanship used as a trophy case for a plastic honorary badge
jokes.explanation: This is a top-three moment in the episode. The shadowbox was established early, Ron was buzzer-dismissed for it, and now it's been repurposed in a way that uses it correctly (displaying an object of value) but wrong for Ron's sensibilities. The single 'No!' does enormous work — it contains Ron's entire relationship with craftsmanship, dignity, and the indignity of having his work co-opted. Perfect callback structure across the episode. 'Son, we spent four days making that' extends the joke beautifully.

jokes.text: Andy, newly badged, immediately demands handcuffs: 'I'm a cop! I should get some handcuffs too! Give me your cuffs, Randy.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just been given an honorary (non-functional) police badge
jokes.punchline: He immediately asserts full police authority, demanding an actual officer's handcuffs — escalating from honorary badge to claiming law enforcement powers
jokes.explanation: The escalation from honorary badge to demanding functional handcuffs is a perfect Andy move. The real officer's exasperated 'No, no. It's an honorary title. Stand down, sir' adds a good straight-man counterpoint. The immediate seizure of authority is character-true.

jokes.text: Andy sees the initials 'J.C.' on the fabric clue and concludes: 'President Jimmy Carter stole my guitar? But why?'
jokes.setup: Professor Smartbrain identifies tiny initials 'J.C.' on a piece of fabric left at the crime scene
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately and confidently concludes the thief is President Jimmy Carter, treating this as a logical deduction
jokes.explanation: The jump from initials to 'Jimmy Carter' is perfectly absurd and completely Andy — he takes the most famous J.C. (ignoring several obvious alternatives) and adds the totally sincere 'But why?' as if Carter's motive is the confusing part. Ben's 'I don't think it's Jimmy Carter, buddy' is a wonderful understatement. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: John Cena arrives, is surprised Andy is an adult: 'From the information I got I just assumed you'd be like 10 years old.'
jokes.setup: John Cena arrives at Johnny Karate's children's show as a surprise guest
jokes.punchline: Cena assumed the host of this show must be a child; Andy thanks him as a compliment
jokes.explanation: The joke is meta — it's commenting on Andy's man-child energy so broadly that a professional guest assumed the host couldn't be an adult. 'Thank you' as Andy's response to being mistaken for a 10-year-old is perfect character. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Andy handcuffs John Cena and drags him to the Funky Monkey Dunk Tank — Cena protests 'I didn't steal his guitar, man. I'm just doing this as a favor.'
jokes.setup: The mystery of who stole the guitar has been building; John Cena's initials 'J.C.' match
jokes.punchline: Andy arrests Cena and drags him to the Funky Monkey Dunk Tank, while Cena — who could easily overpower Andy — protests that he's an invited guest just doing a favor
jokes.explanation: Multiple callbacks firing simultaneously: Macklin cuffs someone, the Funky Monkey Dunk Tank pays off, and the absurdity of John Cena being dragged by Andy Dwyer is visual comedy gold. The implicit visual gag — Cena allowing himself to be manhandled — is the real laugh.

jokes.text: John Cena says 'I don't wanna go in the dunk tank.' Andy: 'Shut up.' Cena: 'Is anybody in charge? Uh, a little help?'
jokes.setup: John Cena is being forced into the Funky Monkey Dunk Tank by Andy
jokes.punchline: The world's most powerful professional wrestler is pleading for help while Andy tells him to shut up
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the power inversion — John Cena could destroy Andy but plays along out of good nature/confusion. 'Is anybody in charge?' from someone who could very much take charge is great.

jokes.text: The karate gi will be displayed somewhere in Pawnee — 'not here here, because this studio actually has a show where divorced couples work out their problems, so that might be weird if that thing was hanging over them.'
jokes.setup: Leslie promises the Johnny Karate gi will stay in Pawnee forever as a memorial
jokes.punchline: She clarifies it won't be in this specific studio because of the divorce mediation show — a perfectly mundane logistical concern undercut by the absurd specificity of the show it hosts
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'divorced couples work out their problems' as a show in this same local studio is a funny worldbuilding detail. Leslie's pragmatic concern about the gi's effect on divorce mediation is a good character note. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Fake Verizon-Exxon-Chipotle merger commercial — three companies announce a 'cross-platform merger' combining wireless coverage, natural gas drilling, and chicken quesadillas.
jokes.setup: An ad begins with inspirational language about energy and attaining goals
jokes.punchline: The 'energy' in question is the product of a merger between a telecom, an oil company, and a fast food chain — a completely insane corporate combination presented with total confidence
jokes.explanation: Sharp corporate satire. The merger of three unrelated megacorporations is absurd, but the comedy is elevated by 'perfecting the chicken quesadilla' being listed as equivalent in importance to 6G coverage and natural gas drilling. Good originality — this predates some real-world absurd mergers. The commercial's earnestness makes the parody land.

jokes.text: Andy's best day ever caveat: 'I once found a rock that looked exactly like Santa Claus. Hat and everything, so...'
jokes.setup: Andy says today is the best day of his life, qualifying 'that's saying something'
jokes.punchline: The thing that has previously competed with this day is finding a Santa-shaped rock, described with the precision of 'hat and everything, so...'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the two or three best jokes of the episode. The joke is multi-layered: Andy claiming something is his 'best day' while implying there's stiff competition, that competition being a rock, and the rock having the impossible specificity of 'hat and everything, so...' The 'so...' trailing off is the crucial element — it implies the Santa hat detail clinches an argument he's making. This is distilled Andy Dwyer. High originality, perfect character integration, economical, earned. Highly quotable. Near the top of the episode.

jokes.text: April's emotional confession: 'Every week this show is an amazing train wreck, and you love doing it, and you're the best host. Like, even better than my all-time favorite host, Tom Snyder, which is crazy.'
jokes.setup: April is having a vulnerable moment confessing her fears about making Andy give up his show
jokes.punchline: In the middle of a heartfelt compliment, she compares Andy to Tom Snyder — an obscure 1970s late-night host — as her personal gold standard for television presenting
jokes.explanation: April's choice of Tom Snyder — a very specific, very niche television reference — as her 'all-time favorite host' is perfectly in character. April would have an idiosyncratic, obscure TV taste. The 'which is crazy' acknowledges the absurdity of the comparison while completely meaning it. Good emotional-comedy blend.

jokes.text: Andy recaps the Five Karate Moves and notes: '...we karate-chopped something, old Mailman Barry's face.'
jokes.setup: Andy is summarizing the episode's Five Karate Moves to Success
jokes.punchline: He describes the 'karate chopped something' achievement as specifically 'old Mailman Barry's face' — with complete blandness
jokes.explanation: The callback lands because of the casual specificity — Barry's face is treated as a neutral, expected object to karate chop. The 'old' adds a small cruelty. Good economy.

jokes.text: Andy's speech to April: 'You're my Verizon-Chipotle-Exxon.'
jokes.setup: Andy is delivering a sincere, romantic speech about why April is his source of strength and energy
jokes.punchline: He compares her to the Verizon-Chipotle-Exxon merger — the fictional monstrosity from the commercial — as the highest energy metaphor available to him
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode and one of the best joke structures in Parks and Recreation as a whole. The Verizon-Chipotle-Exxon commercial was funny on its own, but using it as the climax of Andy's sincere love declaration elevates both jokes. Andy uses the only available 'energy' metaphor he encountered that day — a corporate monstrosity — as a term of endearment. It's perfectly Andy (he means it completely), perfectly structured (callback to the commercial), and somehow genuinely sweet while being absurd. Highly quotable, high rewatch value. This is a top-tier Parks joke. Comparable in quality to the vasectomy anchor example in its perfect character integration and surprise.

jokes.text: After Andy's heartfelt speech, April says: 'Well, that was a very good Being Nice To Someone. I did it. Now I can go finish the show.'
jokes.setup: April and Andy have just had a genuine emotional moment; April was crying
jokes.punchline: April immediately reframes her emotional vulnerability as completing a task — 'Being Nice To Someone' — and walks back to the show, characteristically refusing to dwell in sentimentality
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes, landing immediately after genuine emotion. April has just shown vulnerability; her reframe of it as a completed task ('I did it') protects her persona while also being warmly funny. The clinical phrasing 'Being Nice To Someone' as if it's a chore or achievement to unlock is perfectly April. The joke also works because of the love underneath it — she did do something kind, and calling it a 'Being Nice To Someone' is a wry self-acknowledgment. High character integration, excellent economy, completely earned after the emotional beat. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Final scene: Everyone has left; John Cena is trapped somewhere calling 'Guys? Guys?... Tarantula! Could somebody get me outta here? Please?' — Andy offers to help. Cena: 'No.'
jokes.setup: The episode is ending with the emotional goodbye; the tarantula and dunk tank storylines have been forgotten
jokes.punchline: John Cena is still trapped (presumably in or near the dunk tank) and now also confronted by the loose tarantula; Andy offers to help and Cena refuses — because Andy's help is clearly worse than the tarantula
jokes.explanation: A perfect episode-closing joke that ties together both running gags (tarantula, dunk tank) and adds the final indignity: Andy's help is so untrusted that Cena prefers to handle a 'Devil's Fist' tarantula alone. 'No.' as the final word of the episode is perfect economy. Multiple callbacks firing simultaneously in the tag. Structure score is high because this is a tight, satisfying button that wraps the episode's comedic threads.

tmdb_overview: On the last episode of Andy's TV show, his friends wish him luck with whatever comes next.
insight: Season finale setup sustains 44 jokes across 44 minutes with character comedy driving the late-run momentum.
